notesStmt.note: This manuscript was likely composed in late 1890 or early 1891.

note.p: This is a fragment of a draft of "Have We a National Literature?" which appeared in the March 1891 issue of North American Review. Whitman included it in Good–Bye My Fancy (1891) under the revised title "American National Literature." The manuscript has been affixed, probably by Horace Traubel, one of Whitman's literary executors, to a backing sheet made of letterhead stationery from the office of The Artsman. Traubel's note in the lower right corner is dated 1907 and indicates that he presented this item to Edward Gordon Craig.

body.p: ‸And yet Then Another and very grave point, (for this discussion is not on trifles, or mere seemings—but deep, deep.) I am not sure but the old (and superb and profound and ‸one may say needed as old) conception of Deity as mainly ‸(? merely) essentially of moral construction, (goodness, purity, sinlessness, &c;) has been will be has been undermined by modern 20th century ideas and science. What does this strange almost unhealthy developementdevelopment of philanthropy among the moderns One doubts if there will ever come to be a day when the moral laws and moral standards will be supplanted as ‸ from being over all; as time advances ‸(I find it so in myself.) they will more probably be entrenched deeper and expanded wider. But the scientific ‸and democratic thought and truly ‸philosophic and poetic thought of the moderns advances demands a Deific identity ‸and scope superior to all even ‸ all hitherto that, ‸limitations, and ‸essentially including just as well the e so-call'd evil, and crime and criminals—all the mal-formations, the defective, the abortions.×
